metadata.title: Tax loophole fears cloud UK marketplace VAT reform

content.text:
UK independent retailers warn that proposed exemptions for smaller sellers and second-hand goods could weaken tax enforcement and reduce funding for business rates relief.
Proposed changes to UK online marketplace VAT rules could leave opportunities for tax evasion if exemptions for smaller sellers and second-hand goods are too broad, the British Independent Retailers Association (Bira) has warned.
The association supports plans to extend online platforms' responsibility for collecting value added tax (VAT), but says the final rules must prevent non-compliant sellers from exploiting gaps in the system.
The warning, issued on 16 October ahead of the UK Budget on 28 October, follows reports that platforms such as Amazon, eBay and Temu could become responsible for collecting VAT on more sales made through their services.
The government has consulted on extending marketplace VAT liability to consumer sales by UK-based businesses whose goods are located in the UK when sold. The consultation closed on 18 August 2026, and the proposals remain subject to a government decision.
Seller threshold draws scrutiny
Bira's concerns centre on reports that marketplace VAT collection could apply only to sellers with annual sales above £90,000, while second-hand goods could be excluded.
"The headline is positive, but the devil is in the detail," said Bira chief executive Andrew Goodacre.
The association warned that broad exemptions could weaken enforcement and reduce the revenue generated by the reforms. Bira cited £1bn in potential revenue reported in connection with the plans, although this is not a confirmed government forecast.
The government's preferred consultation option is a £90,000 sales threshold for each marketplace. This would determine when a platform becomes responsible for accounting for VAT on a UK business's sales through that service.
The threshold would not replace existing VAT registration rules, which are based on a business's total taxable turnover across its sales channels. The consultation also considered a lower platform threshold and VAT relief for eligible smaller businesses.
Reform would expand platform VAT duties
Online marketplaces already account for VAT on certain sales involving overseas businesses. These include qualifying imported consignments worth £135 or less and sales to UK consumers of goods already located in the UK, subject to specific conditions and exceptions.
The proposed extension would transfer responsibility for accounting for VAT on eligible domestic marketplace sales from UK sellers to the platforms facilitating those transactions.
